html:
A marble statue of the goddess Aphrodite made by the Athenian sculptor Praxiteles in the 4th century BCE for the city of Knidos in southwest Anatolia. It was one of the first life size statues of a fully nude woman in Greek art.

Until then Greek sculptors showed men nude but women clothed. The story goes that Praxiteles made two versions; the island of Kos chose the draped one, and Knidos took the nude. The goddess is shown about to bathe, one hand held before her body. Her model is said to have been the courtesan Phryne.

The statue stood in a round shrine where it could be seen from every side, and visitors sailed to Knidos just to look at it. Pliny the Elder says a king offered to pay off the city's whole debt for it, and Knidos refused. The original was later taken to Constantinople and is thought to have burned in a fire in 475 CE. Roman copies survive, and it shaped the female nude in Western art for centuries.
